questions.question: Which reagent reacts directly with ethanoic acid to form ethanoyl chloride? Options: A chlorine, B chloroethane, C hydrogen chloride, D phosphorus(V) chloride.
steps: Ethanoyl chloride is an acyl chloride, made by replacing the -OH of the acid with -Cl.
Chlorine and chloroethane do not replace the -OH group of a carboxylic acid.
Hydrogen chloride does not react with the -OH group of ethanoic acid to form the acyl chloride.
PCl5 reacts: CH3COOH + PCl5 -> CH3COCl + POCl3 + HCl, so D is correct.

questions.question: An organic compound, shown as a structure in the original paper, reacts with excess sodium hydroxide solution. What is the organic product?
steps: The compound is HOOCCH=CHCOOH (butenedioic acid), a dicarboxylic acid with two acidic COOH groups.
Excess NaOH neutralises both COOH groups: HOOCCH=CHCOOH + 2NaOH -> NaOOCCH=CHCOONa + 2H2O.
The C=C bond is not affected by NaOH, so B (only one COOH neutralised), C (C=C changed) and D (COOH reduced to CHO) are wrong.

questions.question: Which organic compound reacts with both LiAlH4 and magnesium? Options: A an aldehyde, B a carboxylic acid, C a ketone, D a tertiary alcohol.
steps: LiAlH4 reduces aldehydes, ketones and carboxylic acids to alcohols.
Magnesium reacts with compounds that have an acidic O-H, releasing hydrogen gas.
A carboxylic acid has an acidic O-H, so it reacts with Mg and is reduced by LiAlH4.
Aldehydes and ketones do not react with Mg, and tertiary alcohols react with neither, so B is the only match.

questions.question: Give the mechanism for Step 1, the reaction of ethanal with HCN (with KCN as the source of CN-), including curly arrows, lone pairs and dipoles.
questions.answer: Nucleophilic addition: CN- attacks the delta+ carbonyl carbon, the C=O pi bond moves onto O, then O- takes H+ from HCN, regenerating CN-.
steps: CN- from KCN is the nucleophile; HCN is only a weak source of H+ and CN-.
Curly arrow from the lone pair on C of CN- to the delta+ carbon of the C=O group.
Curly arrow from the C=O pi bond to the oxygen, giving an alkoxide ion with O- and a planar intermediate.
Curly arrow from the O- lone pair onto the H of HCN, giving CH3CH(OH)CN and regenerating CN-.

questions.question: A student predicted that the Step 1 product would rotate plane-polarised light. Comment on this prediction.
questions.answer: Prediction is wrong: the product is a racemic mixture of equal R and S enantiomers, so the rotations cancel and there is no net rotation.
steps: The product CH3CH(OH)CN has one chiral carbon, so it has two enantiomers.
CN- attacks the planar C=O of ethanal equally from above and below the plane.
Equal amounts of the two enantiomers form, which is a racemic mixture.
Equal and opposite rotations cancel, so no net rotation of plane-polarised light is observed.

questions.question: Complete the table summarising Step 2, the hydrolysis of the hydroxynitrile to lactic acid. State symbols are not needed.
questions.answer: Reaction type: hydrolysis. Reagent: dilute hydrochloric acid. Conditions: heat under reflux. Equation: CH3CH(OH)CN + 2H2O + HCl -> CH3CH(OH)COOH + NH4Cl
steps: Reaction type: hydrolysis (acid hydrolysis of a nitrile group, -CN, to a carboxylic acid group, -COOH).
Reagent: dilute hydrochloric acid (or dilute sulfuric acid).
Conditions: heat under reflux.
Equation: CH3CH(OH)CN + 2H2O + HCl -> CH3CH(OH)COOH + NH4Cl, or in ionic form CH3CH(OH)CN + 2H2O + H+ -> CH3CH(OH)COOH + NH4+.

questions.question: Write an equation for the reaction between sodium hydrogencarbonate, NaHCO3, and lactic acid, CH3CH(OH)COOH.
steps: Lactic acid, a carboxylic acid, is a stronger acid than carbonic acid.
The HCO3- ion acts as a base and accepts H+ from the -COOH group.
Products are sodium lactate, water and carbon dioxide gas.
Atoms balance: C4H7NaO6 on each side.

questions.question: Using the two buffer equilibria (shown in the figure below), explain how the blood buffer keeps pH nearly constant when a small increase in H+ occurs.
questions.answer: Extra H3O+ is removed by HCO3- (Equilibrium 1 shifts right), and the H2CO3 formed breaks down to CO2 and H2O (Equilibrium 2 shifts right), so [H3O+] and pH stay nearly constant.
steps: When the concentration of H3O+ increases, Equilibrium 1 (HCO3- + H3O+ <=> H2CO3 + H2O) shifts to the right.
The large reservoir of HCO3- reacts with the added H+, so most of it is removed and [H3O+] and the pH change very little.
The H2CO3 formed decomposes (Equilibrium 2 shifts right) to CO2 and H2O; the CO2 is lost by breathing out, so H2CO3 does not build up and Equilibrium 1 can keep removing H+.

questions.question: A blood sample has pH 7.41. Calculate the ratio of concentrations of the two buffer species.
steps: Ka = [HCO3-][H3O+] / [H2CO3], so [HCO3-]/[H2CO3] = Ka / [H3O+].

questions.question: Give the IUPAC name of lactic acid, CH3CH(OH)COOH.
steps: The principal functional group is COOH, so the parent is an -oic acid.
The carbon chain has three carbons, giving propanoic acid.
The OH group is on carbon 2, which is named as a hydroxy prefix.
Name: 2-hydroxypropanoic acid.

questions.question: Complete the 3D diagrams of the two enantiomers of lactic acid.
questions.answer: Complete both tetrahedral drawings with the same four groups in mirror-image positions, e.g. left: COOH up, CH3 lower-left, OH on the wedge, H on the dash; right: COOH up, CH3 lower-right, OH on the wedge (lower-left), H on the dash (left).
steps: Lactic acid, CH3CH(OH)COOH, has a chiral carbon bonded to four different groups: CH3, OH, COOH and H.
Left-hand diagram: write COOH on the vertical bond, CH3 on the plain lower-left bond, OH on the solid wedge and H on the dashed bond.

Right-hand diagram: the reflection of the left across the dashed mirror line, so COOH on the vertical bond, CH3 on the plain lower-right bond, OH on the solid wedge (lower-left) and H on the dashed bond (left).
The two drawings are mirror images that cannot be superimposed, so they are a pair of enantiomers.

questions.question: State what is meant by racemic lactic acid.
questions.answer: An equimolar (50:50) mixture of the two enantiomers, so it has no net optical activity.
steps: Enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images of each other.
Racemic means the mixture contains equal amounts of both enantiomers.
Equal amounts give a 50:50 mixture of the two forms.
Their opposite rotations of plane-polarised light cancel, so the mixture is optically inactive.

questions.question: Complete the mechanism for the formation of compound X, CH3CH(OH)CN, from ethanal and HCN in the presence of KCN, with curly arrows, lone pairs and dipoles.
questions.answer: Nucleophilic addition: CN- attacks the delta+ carbonyl carbon, the C=O pi bond moves onto O, then O- takes H+ from HCN, regenerating CN-.
steps: CN- is the nucleophile; the C=O bond is polar with a delta+ carbon and delta- oxygen.
Curly arrow from the lone pair on C of CN- to the delta+ carbon of C=O.
Curly arrow from the C=O pi bond onto the oxygen, forming an O- intermediate.
Curly arrow from the O- lone pair to the H of HCN, giving X and regenerating CN-.

questions.question: Write the ionic equation for the hydrolysis of compound X, CH3CH(OH)CN, by dilute acid to form lactic acid. State symbols are not required.
steps: Acid hydrolysis converts the -CN group into a -COOH group.
The nitrogen leaves as the ammonium ion, NH4+, in acidic solution.
Two water molecules supply the oxygens of COOH and the hydrogens needed.
Check: C3H10NO3+ on both sides, so the equation balances in atoms and charge.

questions.question: Explain, with reference to your mechanism in (c)(ii), why the lactic acid formed is racemic.
questions.answer: CN- attacks the planar carbonyl carbon equally from both faces, giving equal R and S forms; hydrolysis does not change this.
steps: The carbonyl carbon of ethanal is trigonal planar and not chiral.
CN- can attack from either face of the planar C=O with equal probability.
This gives equal amounts of the two enantiomers of X at the new chiral carbon.
Hydrolysis does not affect the chiral carbon, so the lactic acid is also racemic.

questions.question: Calculate the mass of lactic acid, HA (Mr 90.0, pKa 3.86), needed to make 1.00 dm3 of aqueous solution with pH 3.00. The list of assumptions is shown in the figure below.
steps: Ka = [H+][A-]/[HA], so [HA] = (1.00 x 10^-3)^2 / 1.38 x 10^-4 = 7.24 x 10^-3 mol dm^-3 (taking [HA]initial = [HA]equilibrium).

questions.question: Explain how the difference between initial and equilibrium concentration of lactic acid affects the mass needed for a solution of pH 3.00. No calculation is required.
questions.answer: More acid must be added than the calculated mass, because some HA dissociates so the equilibrium concentration is lower than the initial concentration.
steps: The calculation uses the equilibrium concentration of undissociated HA.
Some HA molecules dissociate, so less HA remains at equilibrium than was added.
The initial concentration must therefore be higher than the equilibrium concentration.
A greater mass of lactic acid is needed than the calculated value.

questions.question: Give a possible reason why lactic acid is a stronger acid than ethanoic acid.
questions.answer: The -OH group is electron-withdrawing (inductive effect), which stabilises the lactate ion more than the ethanoate ion.
steps: Acid strength depends on how stable the conjugate base is.
The OH group on C2 of lactic acid withdraws electron density through the carbon chain.
This spreads the negative charge on the lactate ion, stabilising it.
The CH3 group of ethanoic acid is electron-releasing, so ethanoate is less stable and the acid is weaker.

questions.question: Complete the equation for the reaction in the titration of methanoic acid with potassium hydroxide: HCOOH + ... State symbols are not required.
steps: Methanoic acid is a monoprotic acid and KOH is a strong base.
Neutralisation gives a salt and water.
The salt formed is potassium methanoate, HCOOK.
Atoms balance on both sides: HCOOH + KOH -> HCOOK + H2O.

questions.question: Using your equation and the titration curve, calculate the concentration of the potassium hydroxide solution. 25.00 cm3 of 0.150 mol dm-3 methanoic acid was used.
steps: The equivalence point is at the middle of the steep vertical section of the curve, at 22.0 cm^3 of KOH.
HCOOH + KOH -> HCOOK + H2O is 1:1, so moles of KOH = 3.75 x 10^-3 mol.

questions.question: Use the titration curve to determine the acid dissociation constant, Ka, of methanoic acid.
steps: Half-equivalence is at 22.0 / 2 = 11.0 cm^3 of KOH, where half the acid has been neutralised so [HCOOH] = [HCOO-].
At this point Ka = [H+], so pH = pKa. The curve reads pH = 3.8 at 11.0 cm^3.
Ka = 10^-3.8 = 1.6 x 10^-4 mol dm^-3 (about 1.4 to 1.7 x 10^-4 allowing for reading the graph).

questions.question: Equimolar aqueous solutions of propanoic acid and sodium propanoate (Ka = 1.3 x 10^-5 mol dm-3) are mixed to make a buffer of pH 4.6. Calculate the volume ratio of propanoic acid to sodium propanoate.
steps: Henderson equation: pH = pKa + log([salt]/[acid]).
4.6 = 4.886 + log([salt]/[acid]), so log([salt]/[acid]) = -0.286.
Equal concentrations mean volume ratio equals mole ratio, giving 1.93 : 1.

questions.question: Compound X, C4H10O, is oxidised to Y, which reacts with ethanol and concentrated sulfuric acid to give ester Z. Which could be the formula of Z? Options: A CH3COOC(CH3)3, B CH3CH2COO(CH2)3CH3, C (CH3)2CHCOOCH2CH3, D CH3CH2COOCH2CH(CH3)2.
steps: X is oxidised to a carboxylic acid Y, so X must be a primary alcohol.
The ester is formed with ethanol, so it must contain an -OCH2CH3 group.
Only option C contains an ethyl ester group, and its acid part, (CH3)2CHCOOH, comes from oxidising 2-methylpropan-1-ol.
Options A, B and D contain tert-butyl, butyl and isobutyl groups, so C is correct.

questions.question: Which acid is produced by hydrolysis of the molecule shown? Options: A 2-hydroxy-3-methylbutanoic acid, B 3-hydroxy-2-methylbutanoic acid, C 3-hydroxy-2,3-dimethylpropanoic acid, D 4-hydroxypentanoic acid.
steps: The molecule is CH3CH(OH)CH(CH3)C#N, a hydroxynitrile.
Hydrolysis turns the nitrile carbon, -CN, into -COOH, which becomes carbon 1 of the acid.
Numbering from COOH: C2 carries the CH3 group, C3 carries the OH group and C4 is the terminal CH3.
The acid is CH3CH(OH)CH(CH3)COOH, 3-hydroxy-2-methylbutanoic acid.

questions.question: Which is the titration curve when sodium hydroxide is added to maleic acid?
steps: Maleic acid is a dicarboxylic acid, so each molecule can lose two H+ and the titration with NaOH has two equivalence points.
The pH starts low (about 2) and rises to about 12 as NaOH is added, so B (pH falling) is wrong.
A shows two steep rises, at about 25 and 50 cm^3. The second volume is twice the first, as expected for a diprotic acid.
C has only one steep rise (a monoprotic acid) and D has three steep rises, so neither fits.

questions.question: Give the IUPAC name for maleic acid. Options: A (E)-but-2-enedioic acid, B (Z)-but-2-enedioic acid, C (E)-1,2-ethenedioic acid, D (Z)-1,2-ethenedioic acid.
steps: Maleic acid is HOOC-CH=CH-COOH, a four-carbon chain with COOH at both ends.
The parent is but-2-enedioic acid, with the C=C between carbons 2 and 3.
Maleic acid is the cis isomer, with both COOH groups on the same side, so it is Z.
Options C and D use ethenedioic acid, which has only two carbons, so B is correct.

questions.question: How do the boiling temperature and the solubility in water of butanoic acid compare with those of hexane?
questions.answer: D: higher boiling temperature and higher solubility in water
steps: Butanoic acid molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other through COOH groups (as well as London and permanent dipole forces), whereas hexane has only London forces, so butanoic acid has the higher boiling temperature.
The COOH group of butanoic acid can also form hydrogen bonds with water, so it is more soluble than non-polar hexane, which cannot.

questions.question: Which compound has the highest boiling temperature? Options: A butanal, B butan-1-ol, C butanone, D butanoic acid.
steps: Carboxylic acids form hydrogen-bonded dimers, which are strong intermolecular forces.
Butan-1-ol hydrogen bonds but has only one O-H per molecule, so its forces are weaker than the acid dimers.
Butanal and butanone have only dipole-dipole forces, with no O-H group for hydrogen bonding.
Butanoic acid therefore has the highest boiling temperature, so D is correct.

questions.question: LiAlH4 is used to reduce the compound shown. Which is the product? Options: A a saturated alcohol, B a saturated carboxylic acid, C an unsaturated alcohol, D an unsaturated ketone.
steps: The compound is but-3-enoic acid, CH2=CHCH2COOH.
LiAlH4 reduces the carboxylic acid group to a primary alcohol group (CH2OH).
LiAlH4 does not reduce an isolated C=C bond, so the product is but-3-en-1-ol, CH2=CHCH2CH2OH, an unsaturated alcohol.

questions.question: But-2-ene-1,4-diol is converted into 2-oxobutanedioic acid in two steps via intermediate W. Identify W and the reagent for Step 2.
questions.answer: D: W is HOCH2CH(OH)CH2CH2OH and the Step 2 reagent is hot acidified K2Cr2O7
steps: Step 1 adds water across the C=C of HOCH2CH=CHCH2OH, giving the triol W = HOCH2CH(OH)CH2CH2OH.
Step 2 must oxidise: both primary alcohol groups become COOH and the secondary alcohol group becomes C=O, giving HOOCCOCH2COOH (2-oxobutanedioic acid).
The oxidising agent is hot acidified potassium dichromate(VI), so D is correct. LiAlH4 (A, B) is a reducing agent, and C is not formed by one step from the diol.

questions.question: Name the two structural isomers of C4H6O2 acids shown in the question.
questions.answer: But-3-enoic acid (left) and 2-methylpropenoic acid, i.e. 2-methylprop-2-enoic acid (right)
steps: Left isomer: CH2=CHCH2COOH, a four-carbon chain with the C=C between carbons 3 and 4, so but-3-enoic acid.
Right isomer: CH2=C(CH3)COOH, a three-carbon chain with a methyl group on carbon 2, so 2-methylpropenoic acid (2-methylprop-2-enoic acid).

questions.topic: E Z Isomers Of Butenoic Acid
questions.question: The third structural isomer of C4H6O2 acids has two stereoisomers. Draw these stereoisomers.
questions.answer: (E)-but-2-enoic acid and (Z)-but-2-enoic acid, CH3CH=CHCOOH (E: CH3 and COOH on opposite sides of C=C; Z: same side).
steps: Of the C4H6O2 carboxylic acids, only but-2-enoic acid can show stereoisomerism.
E/Z stereoisomers arise from restricted rotation about C=C with two different groups on each carbon.
In CH3CH=CHCOOH, each C of the C=C bears H and a different group (CH3 or COOH).
E has CH3 and COOH on opposite sides of the C=C; Z has them on the same side.

questions.question: Draw the fourth structural isomer of C4H6O2 carboxylic acids.
questions.answer: Cyclopropanecarboxylic acid: a three-membered carbon ring (cyclopropane) with a COOH group attached to one ring carbon
steps: The four structural isomers are but-3-enoic acid, 2-methylpropenoic acid, but-2-enoic acid (which has the E and Z stereoisomers) and one more.
The remaining isomer has C4H6O2 with one ring in place of the C=C: cyclopropane carbon ring with COOH attached, C3H5-COOH.
Draw a triangle of three carbon atoms with a -C(=O)OH group on one corner.

questions.question: Give the reagents and conditions for Reaction 1 of 3-hydroxy-3-methylbutanoic acid.
questions.answer: Acidified potassium dichromate(VI), heated under reflux
steps: Reaction 1 converts the primary alcohol group CH2OH into COOH, so it is oxidation.
Reagent: acidified potassium dichromate(VI), K2Cr2O7 with dilute sulfuric acid.
Condition: heat under reflux. The tertiary alcohol group is not oxidised.

questions.question: Write the equation for Reaction 2 of 3-hydroxy-3-methylbutanoic acid. State symbols are not required.
steps: Reaction 2 is acid hydrolysis of the nitrile group, -CN, to the carboxylic acid group, -COOH.
Two molecules of water are needed, and the nitrogen ends up as ammonium chloride with the HCl.
Equation: (CH3)2C(OH)CH2CN + 2H2O + HCl -> (CH3)2C(OH)CH2COOH + NH4Cl. Atoms and charges balance.

questions.question: Give the structure of the organic product formed in Reaction 3 of 3-hydroxy-3-methylbutanoic acid.
steps: PCl5 replaces an -OH group by -Cl, and it reacts with both the carboxylic acid OH and the alcohol OH.
Excess PCl5 therefore converts COOH to COCl and the tertiary C-OH to C-Cl.
The product is (CH3)2C(Cl)CH2C(=O)Cl; HCl and POCl3 are also formed.

questions.question: Give the structure of the organic product formed in Reaction 4 of 3-hydroxy-3-methylbutanoic acid.
steps: Aqueous ammonia is a weak base, so it reacts with the carboxylic acid group by neutralisation.
The product is the ammonium salt (CH3)2C(OH)CH2COO- NH4+.

questions.question: Which compound has the highest boiling temperature? Options: A CH3CH2CH2CH2CH3, B CH3CH2CH2CHO, C CH3COCH2CH3, D CH3CH2COOH.
steps: Carboxylic acids form hydrogen-bonded dimers, the strongest intermolecular force here.
Pentane has only London forces and has the lowest boiling temperature of the four.
Butanal and butanone have dipole-dipole forces but no O-H group for hydrogen bonding.
Propanoic acid, option D, therefore has the highest boiling temperature.

questions.question: What solvent is used for the reaction of the compound shown with excess LiAlH4? Options: A ethanol, B ether, C ethyl ethanoate, D water.
steps: LiAlH4 reacts violently with water and with protic solvents such as ethanol.
Water and ethanol would be attacked by the hydride ions, so they cannot be used.
Ethyl ethanoate would itself be reduced by excess LiAlH4.
Dry ether is an aprotic solvent that does not react with LiAlH4, so B is correct.

questions.question: What is the organic product formed when the compound shown reacts with excess LiAlH4?
questions.answer: D: the unsaturated primary alcohol pent-4-en-1-ol, CH2=CHCH2CH2CH2OH
steps: The compound is pent-4-enoic acid, CH2=CHCH2CH2COOH.
Excess LiAlH4 reduces the COOH group all the way to a primary alcohol, CH2OH; it does not stop at the aldehyde, so A and C are wrong.
LiAlH4 does not reduce the C=C bond, so the double bond remains and the product is pent-4-en-1-ol (option D, not the saturated alcohol B).

questions.question: Which substance is the least soluble in water? Options: A propanal, B propan-1-ol, C propanoic acid, D sodium propanoate.
steps: Propan-1-ol and propanoic acid both form hydrogen bonds with water and are miscible with it.
Sodium propanoate is ionic and very soluble in water.
Propanal can accept hydrogen bonds from water at its C=O group but has no O-H to donate.
Propanal is therefore the least soluble of the four, so A is correct.

questions.question: Which test distinguishes between the first pair of compounds shown? Options: A Tollens' reagent, B sodium carbonate solution, C warm with iodine under alkaline conditions, D phosphorus(V) chloride.
questions.answer: B: add sodium carbonate solution to each compound
steps: The pair is butan-1-ol and butanoic acid.
Butanoic acid is a carboxylic acid and reacts with sodium carbonate to give a salt, water and CO2, so there is effervescence; butan-1-ol does not react.
Tollens reagent and alkaline iodine do not react with either compound, and PCl5 reacts with both (steamy fumes of HCl).

questions.question: Which test distinguishes between the second pair of compounds shown? Options: A Tollens' reagent, B sodium carbonate solution, C warm with iodine under alkaline conditions, D phosphorus(V) chloride.
questions.answer: C: warm each compound with iodine under alkaline conditions
steps: The pair is butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol.
Butan-2-ol contains the CH3CH(OH)- group, so it gives a pale yellow precipitate of CHI3 (triiodomethane) with iodine and alkali; butan-1-ol does not.
Tollens reagent and sodium carbonate do not react with either, and PCl5 reacts with both alcohols.

questions.question: Which test distinguishes between the third pair of compounds shown? Options: A Tollens' reagent, B sodium carbonate solution, C warm with iodine under alkaline conditions, D phosphorus(V) chloride.
questions.answer: A: warm each compound with Tollens reagent
steps: The pair is pentan-3-one (a ketone) and butanal (an aldehyde).
Aldehydes are oxidised by Tollens reagent, giving a silver mirror, while ketones are not oxidised, so only butanal gives a silver mirror.
Neither compound reacts with sodium carbonate or PCl5, and neither contains the CH3C=O group needed for the iodoform reaction.

questions.question: The reaction between ethanoic acid and LiAlH4 is best described as which type? Options: A elimination, B oxidation, C reduction, D substitution.
steps: LiAlH4 is a source of hydride ions, H-, which are reducing agents.
Ethanoic acid is converted into ethanol, with the carbon bonded to oxygen going from +3 to -1.
A decrease in oxidation state, or gain of hydrogen, is reduction.
Option C is correct.

questions.question: Which reducing reagent converts carboxylic acids to alcohols? Options: A acidified potassium dichromate(VI), B concentrated sulfuric acid, C hydrogen gas with a nickel catalyst, D lithium tetrahydridoaluminate(III) in dry ether.
questions.answer: D - lithium tetrahydridoaluminate(III) in dry ether
steps: LiAlH4 is a strong reducing agent that reduces the C=O of COOH to CH2OH.
Acidified dichromate is an oxidising agent and converts alcohols into acids, the reverse of the required change.
Concentrated sulfuric acid is a dehydrating agent or catalyst, not a reducing agent.
Hydrogen with a nickel catalyst does not normally reduce carboxylic acids under these conditions, so D is correct.

questions.question: Identify the reagent and conditions for Reaction A in the scheme involving butanoic acid.
steps: Reaction A reduces the carboxylic acid group COOH to a primary alcohol, CH2OH.
The reagent is LiAlH4 (lithium tetrahydridoaluminate(III)).
The solvent must be dry ether, because LiAlH4 reacts with water.

questions.question: Name the type of reaction taking place in Reaction B of the butanoic acid scheme.
steps: In Reaction B the nitrile group, -CN, of CH3CH2CH2CN is converted to the carboxylic acid group, -COOH, by reaction with water and acid.
This is hydrolysis.

questions.question: Give the structural formula and name of Substance C in the butanoic acid scheme.
steps: Butanoic acid reacts with methanol in the presence of concentrated H2SO4 as a catalyst to form an ester (esterification).
The ester is CH3CH2CH2COOCH3, named from the alcohol (methyl) and the acid (butanoate): methyl butanoate.

questions.question: Identify the reagent for Reaction D in the butanoic acid scheme, and give one observation.
questions.answer: Reagent: phosphorus(V) chloride, PCl5. Observation: steamy (misty) white fumes of hydrogen chloride
steps: Reaction D replaces the OH of the COOH group by Cl, forming the acyl chloride CH3CH2CH2COCl.
Reagent: phosphorus(V) chloride, PCl5 (SOCl2 is also acceptable).
Observation: steamy white fumes of HCl are given off.

questions.question: Write the full equation for the formation of Substance E in the butanoic acid scheme. State symbols are not required.
steps: Butanoic acid is a stronger acid than carbonic acid, so it reacts with sodium hydrogencarbonate in an acid-base reaction.
Substance E is the salt sodium butanoate; water and carbon dioxide are also formed.
CH3CH2CH2COOH + NaHCO3 -> CH3CH2CH2COONa + H2O + CO2 is balanced.

questions.question: Complete the diagram by adding one water molecule to show the strong intermolecular force between butanoic acid and water, including dipoles and lone pairs, and label the force.
questions.answer: Hydrogen bond between the delta+ H of the acid O-H (or of water) and a lone pair on the oxygen of the other molecule, drawn as a dotted line labelled hydrogen bond.
steps: Draw one water molecule, H-O-H, close to the carboxyl group.
Mark the dipoles: delta+ on the H of the acid O-H group and on the H atoms of water, delta- on the oxygen atoms.
Draw a lone pair on the oxygen of the water molecule (or on the C=O oxygen of the acid) pointing to the delta+ hydrogen of the other molecule.
Join the lone pair on one oxygen to the delta+ H on the other with a dotted line, and label it hydrogen bond.
